items.title: Childhood maltreatment and the developing brain: toward individualized models of psychiatric risk
items.author: Haley R. Wang, Carrie E. Bearden, Tiffany C. Ho
items.content: <article>Childhood maltreatment shapes brain development in ways that vary by adversity type, developmental timing, and genetic vulnerability to psychiatric illness—a heterogeneity that conventional approaches capture poorly. We contend that normative modeling, multivariate methods, and polygenic risk scores offer complementary frameworks for parsing this variability and advancing mechanistic insights and clinical stratification.</article>

items.title: From maps to new thoughts: can place-cell indexing generate novel cortical states?
items.author: Stephanie Theves
items.content: <article>Constructing novel states from experience underpins imagination and abstraction. The hippocampal formation is thought to contribute by capturing the relational structure of experiences, but it remains unclear how its abstract relational codes are eventually translated into cortical content representations. I highlight that hippocampal–cortical indexing may scaffold the generation of new states.</article>

items.title: The next generation of fear generalization
items.author: Samuel E. Cooper, Patrick A.F. Laing, Augustin C. Hennings, Bram Vervliet
items.content: <article>Generalizing from past experience is a fundamental feature of cognition. Although generalization has been of long-standing interest to diverse domains in psychological science, the past decade has seen a rapid acceleration of fear generalization research in particular. The field of human fear generalization is at a pivotal juncture where it is now possible to synthesize extensive behavioral work, competing theoretical models, animal and human neuroscience, and clinical and individual-differences research to address enduring gaps. In this review, we provide an updated account of where the field of human fear generalization currently resides and offer concrete avenues for new research emphasizing tighter integration between animal and human neuroscience, prioritizing cross-disciplinary perspectives, and updating conceptual frameworks to align with rapidly advancing methods.</article>

items.title: Language structure as training for executive functions
items.author: Velia Cardin
items.content: <article>Language plays a central role in the development of executive functions (EFs). This forum article discusses how language, as a structured environmental stimulus, can shape EF systems and impact EF outcomes. This has implications for developmental and clinical conditions in which language and EFs are jointly affected, and for congenitally deaf children and adults, who often experience reduced access to natural language during development.</article>

items.title: The nativist–empiricist debate is broken
items.author: Jake Quilty-Dunn, Justin N. Wood
items.content: <article>The nativist–empiricist debate has long organized cognitive science, framing cognitive mechanisms as either innate or learned. Recent advances in controlled rearing and scalable domain-general neural networks now allow this debate to be tested with unprecedented rigor, by raising newborn animals and deep neural networks under tightly matched developmental conditions. Strikingly, when pushed to this empirical limit, the debate does not resolve: the same developmental phenomena support both radical empiricism and radical nativism. We argue that this stalemate reflects a conceptual error. The debate conflates explanatory levels and ontological orientations, with nativists emphasizing stable symbolic structures and empiricists emphasizing the subsymbolic processes that produce those structures. We propose dissolving the dichotomy within a multilevel framework of cognitive development.</article>

items.title: Valuation as a bridge between aesthetics and creativity
items.author: Oshin Vartanian, Martin Skov, Marcos Nadal, Anjan Chatterjee
items.content: <article>Evidence shows that aesthetic evaluations are underpinned by mechanisms in the reward system that compute value for objects of interest. In turn, recent behavioral, computational, and neuroimaging evidence suggests that creativity involves a similar valuation process, as people generate and evaluate the originality and adequacy of their ideas—two standard criteria of creativity. These findings suggest that creativity and aesthetic evaluation may be supported by a domain-general mechanism for computing subjective value. We offer a proposal in which creators’ value computations are conveyed by the structure and content of their works and recovered during aesthetic evaluation through shared reward-system mechanisms and associated processes. On this view, creating and appreciating are two related expressions of a shared value-based process.</article>

items.title: Toward an interdisciplinary mind science of advanced meditation
items.author: Jonathan M. Lieberman, Matthew D. Sacchet
items.content: <article>Meditation research is increasingly moving beyond mindfulness and other early-stage practices toward advanced meditation, encompassing states, stages, and endpoints that progressively unfold with increasing expertise through meditative development. This emerging subfield consists of interdisciplinary research that brings advanced meditation within reach of systematic scientific investigation. Here we articulate this research subfield, including its constitutive conceptual and methodological components and interrelated translational domains: philosophical and theoretical foundations, computational phenomenology, cognitive neuroscience, epidemiology and public health, clinical and well-being outcomes, and relations with psychedelic experiences. This subfield represents an important development for meditation research and the mind sciences more broadly, with implications for health and well-being and for empirical understanding of the human mind.</article>
